summary: For ages 7–8, teach the functions of flowering-plant parts (roots, stem, leaves, flowers) through evidence rather than assertion — the recommended teaching approach for this topic, with DfE KS2 Y3 explicitly supporting investigation of how water is transported in plants. Children should move from naming parts to explaining what each DOES: roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant; the stem transports water upward and holds the plant up to the light; leaves make food using sunlight; flowers make seeds for reproduction. The central recommended teaching move is test-and-consequence — disable or deprive a part and observe what fails — with the classic coloured-water/celery investigation making stem transport visibly real. The highest-priority conceptual target is confronting the 'plants eat soil' misconception by explicitly separating 'roots take in water and minerals' from 'leaves make the food using sunlight'. Keep food-making at the 'using sunlight' level; the photosynthesis equation and xylem/phloem naming are beyond this stage.
misconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil / through their roots' — not recognising leaves make the food using sunlight.
Thinking the stem is only for support, missing its transport role (or vice versa).
Believing roots 'suck up food' rather than water and minerals.
Seeing flowers as decorative rather than the plant's reproductive organs.

activities.title: Plant test-lab: switch each part on or off and watch what happens
steps: Start with a healthy plant and predict what each part does before testing it.

In the on-screen model, remove or disable the roots and observe the result (the model plant droops because it can no longer take in water); restore them and watch it recover. A real plant pulled up and left without water wilts, and its roots cannot simply be put back.
Stand the plant in blue-dyed water and watch the colour travel up the stem and spread into the leaf veins and petals — evidence that the stem carries water from roots to leaves.

Cover the leaves from the light while the plant still has water, and compare it with an identical, equally watered plant left in the light: over time (days to weeks for a real plant) the covered plant becomes pale and weak while the lit plant stays healthy — evidence that the leaves need sunlight to make the plant's food, and that the roots are not pulling ready-made food from the soil.

After each test, state which job it gave evidence for: absorbing water (roots), carrying water (stem), making food using light (leaves). Notice that none of these tests shows anchoring, support or the flower's job of making seeds; talk about those jobs separately, using other evidence.
Pair the dye test with the real celery-in-food-colouring (or white flower in coloured water) classroom investigation as a hands-on complement.
activities.insight: Each plant part has a specific job, and you can gather evidence for it by seeing what fails when the part is removed, deprived, or blocked — function becomes an observed cause-and-effect rather than a stated fact.

activities.title: Tap-each-part diagram: the job behind every structure
steps: Tap each part of a labelled plant diagram to reveal a short animation of its job: roots drawing in water, water rising in the stem, sunlight hitting the leaf to make food, the flower forming seeds.
Read or say the one-line function for each part as it is revealed.
Link each part back to its name from earlier work on naming plant parts, then annotate a labelled diagram with each part's job in your own words.
activities.insight: Every named part of the plant maps to a specific function — structure and function go together.

activities.title: Match and check: part to job
steps: Match each part to its job: roots → absorb water and minerals and anchor; stem → transport water and support; leaves → make food using sunlight; flowers → make seeds.
Answer targeted questions such as 'Which part makes the plant's food?' and 'What do the roots take in?', deliberately rejecting the option that says roots make or suck up food.
Explain the reason for each match, not just the pairing.
activities.insight: Confirm the structure–function mapping and explicitly reject the idea that roots or soil supply ready-made food.

activities.title: Convince the plant scientist: argue from what you observed
steps: Respond in role to a 'plant scientist' who asks you to justify each part's job: 'Convince me the leaves, not the roots, make the plant's food — what's your evidence?'
Cite what you saw in the investigations (the covered plant weakening compared with the plant in the light, the dye climbing the stem) as the reason for each claim.
Answer follow-up challenges, e.g. explain why a plant kept in a dark box could not make food even with plenty of water and soil.
activities.insight: A part's job can be justified from observed evidence — building toward constructing an argument from evidence.

checkQuestion: A plant is growing in a pot of soil on a sunny windowsill. Which part of the plant actually MAKES its food — and where does the plant get what it needs to make that food? Explain how you know.
checkAnswer: The LEAVES make the plant's food, using sunlight (plus water from the roots and air). The plant does NOT take ready-made food from the soil — the roots take up water and minerals, but the food itself is made in the leaves. Full marks put food-MAKING in the leaves and reject 'food comes from the soil'.
